utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mr. Joash Fang who's been with our team for the last two months. He's a graduate of political sciences from the university of Vancouver, Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Yesterday we discussed the significance of those artefacts which could be of assistance had they not been destroyed. Were you in the courtroom when Christopher Lawrence testified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will remember that on pages 22468 I asked you about blindfolds and on that same page Dr. Lawrence answered that many were very similar, that they were made of high quality and expensive fabric, that very few had knots, whereas the others were made of one piece of fabric. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this say to you? Would it be useful if we were able to see those blindfolds, those alleged blindfolds here in the courtroom? What could we conclude on the basis of seeing them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the forensic aspect, it could be considered from two different points of view. Those blindfolds may be just simple pieces of cloth that are used to bandage the forehead or the headbands that are tied around the forehead by soldiers who belonged to a military group or who want to show affiliation to a religion. So that may mean that tying a band around one's head doesn't mean that that person is blindfolded, i.e., that those were pieces of cloth that were made to serve as blindfolds. In that sense, I would like to be able to see how things were found in situ and how they were described in autopsy reports, and then I would be able to tell you more precisely how things were used, when they were used, if they were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Just a quick clarification. At transcript 22468, Dr. Lawrence did say the blindfolds were all quite similar. He didn't say anything about them being high quality or expensive fabric, so I just thought I'd make that clear for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on page 22474 and 22475, which is a few pages further, Mr. Mitchell was in the courtroom, and you will remember that the entire evidence showed, 7273, for example, 22472 and 22473, for example. However, Professor Dunjic has his diary. He made notes of everybody's words when he was in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, you made reference only to a specific page, 22468. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on 22472 there is a reference to some knots, which means that the blindfolds were not made of a single piece of fabric, whereas the rest of them were made of a single piece of fabric. And then on 22474 and 22475 it says that they were made of a glossy fabric, that some were multi-coloured, that some had patterns, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, you intimated that one cannot draw a conclusion as to whether somebody was killed in fighting and then subsequently buried or buried earlier or whether the body was picked up from the surface. I'm going to tell you what Witness 045 stated. Witness 045 said, let me try and find the page, this is 22674, yes. And I'm going to read in English. The question was this: [In English] "And how was that, were there any casualties? "A. Many casualties. I just mentioned that only in the night of the 12th to the 13th I saw 40 to 50 people who were seriously wounded who were brought to that hill. I don't know what happened to those people later. I didn't hear about that from anyone, and those people were never seen again. "Q. Were they just wounded? Nobody was killed? "A. There were so many killed that nobody could carry them out from the creek, no one could have saved these people. Definitely a large number were killed." [Interpretation] And then the following question: [In English] "Thank you. Is it correct that nevertheless you were aware that a part of 281st Brigade numbering about 1.000 fighters and 500 civilians" -- "A. Well, it's a bit" -- no. "Q. Did you bury the people who had -- killed in fighting in these -- Potoci? "A. Well, it's a bit of a silly question, if I may say that. How could we have time to bury anyone when you don't even know what will happen to you in the next minute? We didn't even have time to look at anyone. "Q. Who buried these people? "A. Nobody ever did unless they were found later or the Serbs gathered them and put them in a mass graves. All the rest are probably still there in those woods." [Interpretation] How does this tally with your findings and your conclusions based on documents as well as the description of the biological material?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert who is in a position to judge the credibility of evidence. It's up to the Court and the Prosecutor. However, as a forensic expert, based on this statement I can single out some elements, one of them is that there was a lot of casualties, a lot of wounded and killed who were not buried. That fact alone, if it indeed is a fact, tallies with what I said earlier and that is that some bodies were subsequently brought to certain locations to the nearest places where they could be buried and that they were already in the stage of putrification. This actually proves what I highlighted in the Prosecutor's witness Dusan Janc. He actually said the same thing, that people were buried subsequently, that the bodies were subsequently brought, and that they were already putrefied. I can regard the evidence of the witness that you have just read out only through that aspect, and obviously in the written part that I submitted to you I quoted some other witnesses who were not protected whose testimonies I received. I cited their findings in the segment which shows how the survivors had been wounded. That was important to me. I wanted to see whether the wounds that were recorded in the autopsy reports correspond somewhat to the stories that the witnesses told us, the survivors who came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same witness confirmed that at least five, if not six, people were killed next to him. They were on the lists of the ICMP as executed and their bodies were found in various graves. If we are going to read their names, I would like to do it in private session, but I don't think we should read the names. Number 1.700, 4.647, 3.489, number 11200 or 112199, 3072, these are the people who were killed next to him and their bodies were found in various mass graves. How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what those numbers are Dr. Karadzic just read out, and I'd also like a cite for the confirmation that at least five or six people were killed next to him and that these are on the lists of the ICMP as executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we -- we don't need to go into private session, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, no. I don't think we have to go to private session. However, this is somewhat later than the first reference I gave you for Witness 045. I did not make a note, so if you will bear with me. This can be found, the names can be found in 65 ter 3246. I believe that the document has been admitted on page 3, 3246 on page 3, and in his testimony it was confirmed that the names were based on the names of the parents, but I have to find that page. After the break I will be able to give you the exact transcript page. The names are there and in the transcript he mentioned the names of the parents, or rather, the fathers and we established that we're talking about the same people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, this was a response to Mr. Mitchell's remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the names are at transcript 22677 and the next page, so there's no need to look for that cite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, your report is very clear and extensive so I will not go through all the details. I would like to ask you this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D9311 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what conclusion would you draw from the fact that the bodies of people who were killed in 1992, 1994, and 1995 were exhumed from just one mass grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can see now in this document is very remarkable. It is striking and significant because it confirms what Dusan Janc wrote in his corrigendum about subsequent burials, about bodies that were brought from different parts, about digging secondary graves, which in my mind are mostly primary mass graves and they are secondary for only some body parts. The most important thing here is that bodies were found in various locations and on the right-hand side you can see exactly what locations those are. This is the list of mass graves, and in the middle there is the date of birth, the name of the person, their father's name, and the date of death pursuant to Brunborg, and the date of birth and date of death according to lists of BiH army. In my mind this was a striking piece of information, i.e., that for one and the same person it may be said that he was killed on the 12th of July, 1995, and that same person, for example, Avdo Ademovic, whose father's name was Taib, was killed on the 1st of August, 1993. As a matter of fact, when I was working on those reports I had seen some tables compiled by the ICMP and some other documents and I could see that those lists contained the names of people who died in 1993 or in 1994. During the Popovic et al. trial it was -- this list was disclosed and actually Geoffrey Nice, who was the Prosecutor in the Milosevic case, asked from the BiH authorities to submit the list of the names of the people who were killed before July 1995, before the fall of Srebrenica. They received a long list containing the names of over 100 people. This is just one part of that list and that list contains the names of the people who were army members and who had been killed previously. It is a well-known fact that there were clashes around Srebrenica even before July 1995. I was asked where the bodies of those people are, the bodies of the people who were killed before July 1995. I said I don't know, and then they said they were found in those mass graves. And then I say, "Yes, they were found in the mass graves, they were identified; however, what I can confirm is the fact that those mass graves contained the bodies of the people in various stages of putrefaction." Because of that I wrote on several occasions and I said on several occasions that the procedure to describe the degradation changes on the bodies that were exhumed is a very significant process because it indirectly confirms the time of death, or rather, the time of burial. And when we were talking about primary and secondary graves, that was not just a theoretical consideration, it was very important because some bodies were completely disjointed which points to a high degree of putrification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further. Professor, do you know who compiled or produced this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. It was presented to me as it is now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is an ERN number from the EDS collection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'll allow me to emphasise one point that I neglected to mention, you have here the date of death by Brunborg and the date of death according to the BiH army list. Now, the date of death indicates the day when a person died. The date of death can be established in various ways. In addition to forensic methods, which are the most important methods, the date can also be established based on witness statements, documents that can be retrieved, and other sort of evidence. This is what I discussed. Now, what I have been doing so far is that a number of cases of individuals exhumed from these mass graves led me to suspect that different times of death or dates of death were recorded because you cannot find in one single mass grave an individual who is -- whose body is fully skeletonised and another body which is only saponified. So this is not consistent with what would normally be found in a mass grave as Richard Wright claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see any BH army lists with their information as to the times of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received from the Defence team for Mr. Vujadin Popovic the entire file of lists with various names and places where these individuals were killed, including the membership of their units at the time and places of death. This is something that the Defence received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these names consistent with the names that you saw on the lists provided by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me tell you that I did this at my own initiative and I tried to match them as far as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at number 128, handwritten, Avdic, Cancari Road 11, date of death 1992. In that same grave, bodies were recovered of individuals who were killed at a later date. In fact, there is almost not a single mass grave that did not contain bodies which died prior to July 1995. What is your conclusion on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only conclusion that I can give as a forensic expert is that the bodies which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you are dealing with what you think is important evidence, do not, please, lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am seeking an explanation from the Professor for the fact that almost all the graves contained bodies with a time of death from different periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In fact, does this list show that, does this list show that there are in mass graves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's leading very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inadvertently. Believe me when I say that it's not deliberate. I simply don't know how to formulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this list indicate with regard to the place of death and time of interment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what the point is about. The list containing times of death indicates that some of these bodies, if they were interred in these graves in 1995 or shortly before the events of July 1995, would have had to have been in an advanced stage of decomposition, putrefaction, and skeletonisation, that's under number 1. Now, two, the fact that there are many cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please help us, the Judges, understand this chart first. By way of example you referred to Avdic, handwritten number 1 to 8 is written to the right of the name. Could you read through the columns and what they signify. Avdic, Hamdija probably first name, correct, Professor? Do you see the chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do see it. Hamdija, father's name Ramiz, 128, born on 16 July 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, please continue. If you touch the screen -- yes, but we would like to see the whole row.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll try to read from here. So Avdic, first name Hamdija, father's name Ramiz, born on the 16th of July, 1971. Date of death, 18 July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's according to Brunborg. Now, the BH army list, date of birth 16 July 1971, so it's the same, but the date of death registered is 15 July 1992. This body was recovered in the mass grave Cancari Road 11 and this is the ID protocol. The recovery of bodies in different locations, having in mind the two dates of death, one according to Brunborg and the other according to the BH army list, clearly indicates that the bodies retrieved here are killed in different places and the bodies were buried in different places, i.e., in the location where they were found, which as a result confirms the thesis that they were killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Date of birth, left -- to the left of Brunborg, date of death. On what document -- basis was it based upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were individuals identified under these names. I don't know who identified them and in what way. Was this information that was provided to the ICMP, first name, last name, father's name, and date of birth, and that was how these persons were being sought, and after that DNA tests were done and identification followed. This is the procedure followed by the ICMP when identifications were made as far as I know. Quite a different matter is how the BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- arrived at the information contained on the list. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could be brief in answering the question. Could you read out the title? We don't have the translation so that we can understand the document. Could you read out the first line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first line, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Primeri identif ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "Examples of identified individuals from the Prosecution list and database of the BH army (for the cases of soldiers killed or gone missing before July 1995 only)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, you said you didn't know about the provenance of this document. Did you yourself confirm that the data cited in this document are consistent with the raw material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to locate some of these cases in the autopsy reports and I wanted to establish on the basis of autopsy reports what I was able to establish, that's to say the degree of putrefaction and to then analyse in that context the times of death, whether the information provided by Brunborg or that information provided by the BH army would be closer to the state of affairs. I established that the putrefaction was so marked and prominent that as a forensic expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I would be inclined to go with the date of death as provided by the BH army list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether, for example, the date of birth and the date of death as cited here were consistent with the ABiH material, whether you checked the data yourself? So the answer seems to be no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't double-check the date of birth or date of death. I was rather comparing the two dates of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that, as indicated by Mr. Karadzic, this document bears the 65 -- the ERN number, whether, Mr. Mitchell, you can assist us as to the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I can, Mr. President. This was annex 3 to the Defence expert report in the Popovic case from Svetlana Radovanovic, who was a demographer called by the Defence teams, which leads me to another point, Mr. President. I think this list is best addressed with someone with expertise in demography, which is clearly not Professor Dunjic's expertise. I'm not sure -- I will double-check. I'm not sure if it was addressed specifically with Dr. Tabeau or with Dr. Brunborg in this case already, but I'll double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have this ABiH material? Could you read out the columns, Mr. Dunjic, Dr. Dunjic, "spisak armije BiH," could you read that out so we could hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out the lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no, the title, title of that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "BiH army list."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Just that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And beneath that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We heard. We know that. Mr. Mitchell, do we have that material, BiH army list, in evidence in our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's in evidence in this case, Mr. President. I know we do have it and I know that the Prosecution demographers have specifically analysed that data against the missing list. I will check for you, though, whether it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic. What is important to check the veracity of this document instead of jumping into the conclusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here let's look at this, the time of death at Cancari Road 11 was July 1992, and I mean Avdic that we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cancari Road 11. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this entry concerning Cancari Road 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's not the next page or -- one more page, please. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the time of death according to Brunborg and what is the date of death according to the BH army in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdic Hamdija, Ramiz, according to Brunborg is 18 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Who are we talking about now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the deaths of two bodies buried at Cancari Road. According to Brunborg, one date was 18 July 1995 for one body and for the other 13 July 1995, and according to the BH army it was 1992 and 1994 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are looking at page 3 now, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the first one is the case that we were reading about previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see two entries on this page related to Cancari Road 11. One is Muminovic and the other is Ramic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant Muminovic, the one at the top, the fifth or sixth from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that was my point. But Professor read out the Avdic entry on page 1. Please continue. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how -- if you just stick to Brunborg, how were the bodies found that died on the -- of the person that died on the 18th and of the person that died on the 13th of July, 1995, allegedly in Cancari Road 11? This is a difference of five or six days. Did you find data that the burials lasted that long?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one second, please. Allow me to look at the list. Muminovic, according to Brunborg, 13th of July, 1995, 13th of July, 1995, Cancari Road number 11, and then Cancari Road for Admir Ramic -- ah, yes, all right. Avdic, it's the 11th of July -- it's the 18th of July, 1995. So if I understood the question how is it possible that the two bodies were buried in a period of five days, there's a difference of five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, Professor. It was heard here in the courtroom that there were no executions before the 14th. There was a person who died on the 13th was found on Cancari Road 11 and a person who was allegedly killed on the 18th was also found in the same grave. Do you ever an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a misrepresentation of the evidence. There's been plenty of evidence that there were executions before the 14th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, none of those -- the evidence did not hold, even Janc said so himself. But let's look at something else and then we'll see later what the B&H army says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Avdic, according to Brunborg, died on the 18th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are you going back to the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm comparing it. The first page and the next one. Avdic killed on the 18th of July was found in the Cancari Road 11 grave. 18th of July. And Muminovic, page 3, 13th of July, Muminovic Dzemal, 13th of July, was found -- not Muminovic, Bajro Dzemal -- Dzemal, son of Bajro.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was found in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only way I can interpret that, if that is correct, if that is correct, that those dates are correct, for the time of death all I can say is that these were burials that were carried out successively, meaning that at one and the same location there were subsequent burials carried out and that would be evidence of subsequent burials or of people found who had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm just confused. If you could assist us, either of you, Cancari Road is one of the primary graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Secondary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, both of these persons according to information by the B&H army, Avdic in 1992 and Muminovic in 1994, these are the dates given for their death.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Professor, you are not in the position to confirm -- so you are not in the position to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I'm not in the position to confirm that. I just simply don't have an explanation as to why there are two dates. As an expert witness what I can say is that there is a lot of evidence, forensic evidence, that bodies were buried subsequently in these secondary and primary graves, that they were brought from different areas, and in my view that is the key. That is why I said what I said yesterday, that the list of people related to the events in Srebrenica in July 1995 is not correct, that there are many more bodies on the list than there were people who died in connection with Srebrenica itself in July 1995. And this is just one more piece of evidence that there was subsequent burials in the primary and secondary graves, that bodies were brought to those graves that were found in the broader area of Srebrenica that are not directly connected to Srebrenica. As for how the army authorities at that time established these things, the way the army was at that time, I believe that this was done by officers who were given a certain assignment to make lists on a daily basis for those who were killed in the army, when, where, in which circumstances, and what was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's finish with this document. Did you see lists of the B&H army and do they correspond to the names that are given in this collection here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the lists in electronic form, both in printed forms, big piles like this, but I did not have the physical possibility or enough time to compare each one and to go through each one. Who knows what else is there on that list. Of course I am not even expert enough myself in order to be able to check all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do some of those names appear on this list as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of those names do appear on this list, and as for what the Prosecutor Mitchell said, first of all, we were there together so I know who worked for the Vujadin Popovic Defence. This was done by a demographer, this is true, but all the Defence lawyers gave this to me, asking me to explain why there were two dates of death. I'm not there as a demographer but as a forensics expert to explain to them how is it possible to find at one location the body of a person who died three years prior to the Srebrenica events and that is the basis on which I draw my conclusion that these people were killed somewhere in fighting elsewhere and that they were later found and subsequently buried there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic is asking the Chamber whether this first report that we have been discussing up until now can be admitted prior to moving to the second report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I misunderstood. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3893, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, sir, to introduce this document. I asked a few concise questions, and so I would like to ask you -- and I asked you to reply to them. So the document deals with the main objections on your part from the point of view of forensics regarding the findings of OTP experts on establishing the cause of death. This is under 1 on page 2. Could you briefly just tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to be as brief as possible about what I put on the report. This report was drafted in relation or in comparison to previous reports and in response to questions that you specifically formulated. As an expert, I tried to make an overall analysis about the things that I as a forensics specialist had objections to. The main and basic thing is that the material is very voluminous and that reports were submitted here through OTP experts, which I also listened to. These are joint reports representing specific locations. These joint reports were drafted on the basis of certain individual reports that were done by different people, different pathologists, and forensics experts. What I was bothered by the most, not only as a forensics expert but -- not only myself but I believe that that would be shared by most forensics experts in the world is that the conclusions were drafted on the basis of some assumptions about the cause of death. The cause of death is something that has to do with disease or injuries that would cause the cessation of all the vital functions of a human organism. These vital functions, if their cessation was caused by injuries, would mean that they were inflicted when the person was still alive. I will gradually explain this. These changes caused during life can be found on the human body around the injury and in all the other parts of the body or organs which respond in a particular way. Based on these reactions, on soft and hard tissue and organs, especially the respiratory, digestive, and central nervous system organs, we establish these changes. The experts who worked here worked in such a way that they adopted an assumption that all these people had to have been alive before that, which is logical, and all those on whom injuries were found died as a result of these particular injuries. However, this is just an assumption and what should provide proof to the Court are the injuries which must undoubtedly be so described and presented so that it can be seen that it was precisely these injuries that led to death. Why is this important in this specific case? We have two aggravating circumstances here: Bodies which were dug out, exhumed, after three, four, or more years which had already been completely skeletonised or had decomposed to such a degree that it was impossible to establish those reactions of the tissue when the person was still alive in order to be able to establish that a particular injury on the head or on the chest was actually the cause of death. In his reports, John Clark and Christopher Lawrence, I mostly talk about them as colleagues who are in the same profession and have the same level of education that I do, they said that in their introduction. But what ensued was that setting off from that assumption that those people were alive at the time of injuries, all the injuries they had found from fire-arms or from some other instrument, they considered them to be ante-mortem injuries and then this was later adopted by the anthropologists Baraybar and Haglund, which may not necessarily be true. They can confirm that something like this is possible but they are not forensics medical experts. So setting off from the assumption that these were caused ante-mortem, they declared all injuries as such and only for a minimal number they said were created post-mortem and then for a certain smaller number they said that they were created immediately prior to death. I cannot accept such a division. I believe that it's -- it was absolutely essential that injuries that were noted should be described and that these findings would need to be consistent with the conclusions. When I say that, I would try to present it in the following way. A head injury which can be described as missing bone sections in a skeletonised body, in one case it's declared to be an ante-mortem injury caused during life and that that was the cause of death. In a similar, different, case with the same defect of the skull bone it is declared as a post-mortem injury or it is described in such a way that it is said that an injury which would correspond to a gun-shot wound, for example. And precisely for that reason, precisely for that reason, in the previous cases and in this one, I wanted to show you something, what that means, simply so that this could be clarified. Is it possible to show these photographs? Is it possible to put this on something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please put the photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show you this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is this part of his report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the first report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload it for the benefit of reference in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not in colour.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Here you have it. It's on page 5 of the additional report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be displayed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the main report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the subsequent report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one that we already have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So far I have been talking about the consistency of findings or the lack thereof. What does this mean? It is inconsistent if it says that this injury is the defect of the frontal part of the skull and the face without any precise description. However, this is how all the pathologists described injuries in their findings. And if you write it like that, you don't know as lawyers, as legal experts, how this injury came about. I can tell you that this injury was caused by fire-arms or perhaps somebody hit somebody else with a baseball bat and caused the injury. But I know because I was the one involved in this case. When you describe this injury in great detail, you will arrive at the conclusion that this murder was committed by an axe. This person was killed with an axe because the edges are sharp and straight and there were wounds on the soft tissues which is lacking at this moment. Therefore, this is what I insist on when I talk about consistency. Describe the injury and then tomorrow we will all be able to arrive at the same conclusion. The pathologist that worked on that described the injuries and said that the injuries were consistent with gun-shot wounds. I don't have the means to verify that. This is the consistency or the lack thereof. Second of all, this is the appearance of a skeletised skull. For this injury to be declared as the cause of death, that injury had to be inflicted the moment when the person was still alive. If that person was not alive but, for example, had died of a heart attack and then somebody grabs an axe and hits that person with an axe, the injury would be the same but that would not have been the cause of death. That's why we as forensic experts insist on ante-mortem, peri-mortem, and post-mortem details in order to be able to establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find in the materials that you perused, and Dr. Lawrence spoke about that on page 2248 and 2249, if, for example, you come across a skeletonised body with or without traces of a projectile from fire-arms, can you tell us whether one can conclude how that person died -- whether that person died in fighting or whether that person was executed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever you come across soft tissue defects or hard tissue defects implies certain morphological changes based on which a forensic expert analyses all of the other traces on the body and around the body or on the site where the body was found and such an expert can reconstruct the trajectories of projectiles and the wounds. And based on that, it may be assumed - it cannot be claimed, it may be assumed - whether some of the injuries were inflicted when the person was facing the assailant or whether he had his back turned to them. All of the injuries that may be caused by fighting are the same as may be seen as a result of execution. All that depends on the given situation. In any case, there are many injuries here that point to the fact that the person was injured during conflict, during fighting. There are a lot of injuries here which were inflicted by various means, ranging from projectiles to shells, shrapnel, and things like that. This implies that nobody is executed by shelling. Shelling is a result of war activities. People are executed by long-barrelled rifles or machine-guns. I apologise. So what I am saying as a forensic expert is that the diagnosis of an injury has to be supplemented with the channels and trajectories and the distances from which it was fired in order to be able to establish the position of the person who was injured vis-a-vis the position of the fire-arms that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question on page 2248 or 2249 was answered by Dr. Lawrence in this way: In a large number of cases he was not able to determine the cause of death. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you should pause like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question properly, you said that Dr. Lawrence stated that in a large number of cases he could not establish the cause of death. This is correct. This is only correct thing. In such circumstances where the bodies were putrefied and when exhumations are -- were carried out years after the burial, it is impossible to establish the causes of death. We can only assume. We can tell the Court: You know, Judge, this is a possible cause of death but we cannot conclude with any certainty that a person who was exhumed after such a long time died of a certain cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We understand your objections; however, within the team itself, among the pathologists, forensic experts, and anthropologists, were there disagreements about the manner in which the task was carried out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the situation was in the field. I did have an opportunity to see Mr. Haglund in 1996 at Ovcara. I -- shall I stop here? Is there a problem? I had an opportunity to read all of their reports. I listened to them on two occasions here in this courtroom. Mr. Lawrence at one point here when he spoke about Cancari Road said something that I couldn't agree with as a forensic expert. I don't know if he said what he really meant. However, he wrote the following about Cancari Road number 3 under bullet point 12: There were a lot of head injuries, rib fractures, and pelvis fractures which were intentionally inflicted post-mortem in order to cover-up the injuries that were inflicted on the same parts of the body peri-mortem. This is on page 4 of the report and I referred to it for a simple reason. I just wanted to say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it might be helpful to look at Dr. Lawrence's report. It doesn't actually say about injuries being intentionally inflicted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please. Cancari Road 3, everything that I put in my report are quotes from the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is ERN number 00920597.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 0597.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0597, after 2, 0597.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 12 and here you have it. This is here and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not helpful. Can we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Dr. Lawrence's report, the original, is -- had 65 ter 2472.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we will use the ERN number to help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We need the first page -- second page, 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Where can we find the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 12 [Interpretation] Under bullet point 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where can we find the passage "intentional"? Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's possible just a translation issue but Professor Dunjic is talking about point 12. He talks about it in his report as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out number 12, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bullet point 12 in the translation: "There were many post-mortem injuries of the skull, ribs, and pelvis which were intentionally inflicted post-mortem in order to cover up peri-mortem injuries inflicted on the same parts of the body."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably there seems to be an issue with translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There could be. I'm not sure that Professor Dunjic has quite accurately quoted the B/C/S translation of this in his report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Dr. Dunjic, you can read English, can't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can read out in English there, which is original, which appears on the right side of the computer -- the monitor which seems to be different from what you read in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't know how to precisely translate the following phrase: [In English] "... pelvis which would tend to obscure peri-mortem injury in these regions." [Interpretation] I don't know how to translate this. I was relying on the Serbian translation. However, irrespective of that, Judge, irrespective of the fact that something was done intentionally or non-intentionally, to claim that some injuries were inflicted subsequently for whatever reason, I as a forensic expert have to know and I have to have elements for such a claim. When did injuries occur? Which ones were the first and which ones were the last? So even if we disregard the term "intentional infliction," if we just concentrate on things that happened post-mortem and what the objective was, then my question to Lawrence would be this: How did you establish the sequence of injuries and the sequence of their inflictions -- infliction? Could those injuries be -- have been inflicted simultaneously? Were they inflicted by one or several persons and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When I asked you about the disagreements within the teams - and you'll find it on page 3 - can you tell us something about the panel in San Antonio and that disagreement. What were the objections proffered by the team members themselves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the last time and I also included this in my report. I was quite surprised, to use the understatement, I was quite surprised when I heard the fact that Mr. Haglund included in all of his reports, and we are talking about the Cerska document dated 15 June. That fact was that post-mortem examinations started on the 31st of July, 1996, you'll find it on page 3. That they lasted until 22nd August 1996. Post-mortems were carried out in makeshift morgues in the Kalesija textile factory which had been damaged during the war. Post-mortems were supervised by Dr. Robert Kirschner who was the director of the international forensic programme of the Medecins Sans Frontieres. When they defined the final conclusion about the cause of death and when they redacted the final version of post-mortem reports, they were helped by a legal expert of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up page 3 in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legal expert Peter McCloskey. Whereas "the summary of all the pathological reports was authored by Dr. Page Hudson," end of quote. William Haglund is the author of these words in his report on page 11 and this is his report on Cerska -- the year was 1968, page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be helpful, it's 1D25488, rather than this document, 1D25488.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Professor, can you tell us the following. The whole process of reconciling different opinions, the assistance provided by Mr. McCloskey, how could this entire procedure have influenced the accuracy of all the findings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now we have the right page. Please have a look at what I quoted. It's the third passage from the top, William Haglund. First of all, this is absolutely unacceptable professionally speaking. It is unacceptable for professionals, physicians, making up a joint team to have their opinions which may be made consistent or they maybe agreed upon their mutual opinions, but to have their opinions redacted or edited in any way afterwards. In this case it was done by a legal advisor, Mr. Peter McCloskey. The only conclusion that I may draw is that this was done deliberately. It's not just my conclusion that I arrived at - Mr. Haglund didn't like it - but it was also the international symposium held at San Antonio that took note of that. And I think that Mr. Mitchell is aware of this, we discussed this the other time in the Popovic case. Serious objections were voiced against such a practice. My colleagues across the world did not want to take part in teams such as this one. Many of my colleagues refused to take part in the work of the team in Bosnia, precisely because they did not want to have their work being corrected, redacted, edited, et cetera. Everyone needs to take responsibility for their own work. So when I came across this section, I wrote this in my report. I am not surprised at the fact that the conclusions about deaths are so uniform although they stand in contradiction to autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, does this document -- that Mr. McCloskey edited the report himself? Does this document say that Mr. McCloskey edited the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it says here in the formulation of a final conclusion about the cause and manner of death as well as in editing the final formulation -- as well as editing of final autopsy report was facilitated by the legal advisor, Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How -- what do you understand the meaning of "facilitation"? How do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what happened in my opinion and what I'm telling you now is my personal opinion. All the forensic officers who were engaged in that exercise had gone through such training that I went through and this is that when you have a skeletonised body you don't know the cause of death. In that case, what you would write down in your conclusion under number 1 is precisely this, that the corpse is in such a stage of decomposition that an accurate cause of death cannot be established, full stop. Under 2, you would say that an autopsy carried out on a putrefied or skeletonised body, such and such injuries originating from such and such mechanism were noted. Then under 3, according to some schools of forensic medicine, you may possibly write what could possibly have been the cause of death, which means that if the injuries under number 1 of the conclusion were inflicted ante mortem, then they could have led to the person's death. So again this is written as an assumption or hypothesis. And most of the forensic physicians would formulate this conclusion. However, what this requires is a different sort of approach. I believe that the legal advisor wanted to skip many a step and to directly tie-in his conclusion -- the conclusion with what he was able to see on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object at this point. This is just rank speculation now, and you've heard evidence from Dr. Haglund at transcript 23940 on what actually happened. So I think Professor Dunjic should stick to his expertise for the remainder of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I think that this was in response to a question put by the Presiding Judge. I'm responding to the objection by Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Meaning of "facilitation." The Chamber is of the view that we heard enough. Shall we move on? Given the time, shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put one more question? Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, further down the text you quote the remarks by Dorothy Gallagher, Yvonne Milewski, David del Pino, and others. Their comments with regard to the influence made on the conclusions and findings, are they consistent with what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went precisely to state the reasons for their discontent, which was exactly what I said, that there was too much subjectivity and too little objectivity.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, this is from the Vujadin Popovic et al. case and it's an official confirmation that this person - I don't want to say the name - was marked as Srebrenica Potocari 1/1 has been determined to have committed suicide. So it's not a Srebrenica victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. But just to be very clear, this individual didn't commit suicide in 1994. He killed himself on the 12th of July, 1995, in Potocari. He is buried in a single grave completely separate from the nine bodies at issue in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably this document speaks for itself. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3895, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D9315, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this letter by Gordon Bacon, head of the ICMP office, addressed to Husein Jakupovic of the Una-Sana canton, and can you please read the first sentence of the second paragraph for us, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to familiarise the Trial Chamber with the broader context of this answer, Mr. Gordon Bacon, who I believe I know because he did come to my institute, this was in 2003 -- the letter is from 2003. In Sarajevo, over there, the ICMP was working on certain identifications and he as the head of ICMP in Sarajevo and Bosnia, of their programme for identification of missing persons, received objections from families and from some other people who worked in these identification centres and, among other things, there were letters from Mr. Odobasic and others who were working on the identification of missing persons. And so then he answers them, replies to these objections of theirs. And now I'm going to try to read that to you. "However, the case cannot be closed only based on DNA structures match. Experienced police inspectors, pathologists, anthropologists, and other experts have to put significant efforts for the identification process to be done in accordance with the highest standards and to help families to find out about the destiny of their missing beloved ones ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Odobasic who also disagreed with the work. Where is Odobasic from? From which -- from which circle of participants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is getting a long way from Professor Dunjic's expertise as a pathologist. He's now testifying about ICMP and we're about to get into allegations made against ICMP. It's got nothing to do with his expertise. These were questions for Dr. Parsons, if anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that now we're not dealing with the DNA, but we are beginning to deal with a general picture of disputing the work that preceded the expertise of Mr. Dunjic. Thus, everything that was done earlier was subject to objections by other instances, by other participants, objections that are similar to those stated by Professor Dunjic in his expert report and which substantiate the conclusions of Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not knowing the content of this document, I'm not fully convinced why this was to be led by Mr. Dunjic. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has doubt whether -- that this is related to his expertise. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Eva Klonowski is and what is her field expertise and what did she do in these processes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that she worked as an anthropologist in the process of identifications at the beginning of the work in 1996 in Bosnia and Herzegovina at these localities. She worked as an expert engaged by the International Tribunal, and she assisted in the identifications in the period before laboratories were set up for DNA identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who is Jasmin Odobasic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him, but I see from the letter that it's a person who was the head at the level of some republican -- I don't know what he was, some kind of republican desk officer for, what do you call them, missing persons, for finding them, president. He actually stated a series of objections to the work of Madam Klonowski and some other associates because there were many complaints about identifications that had been carried out that -- so far. Because of erroneous identifications, the families did not want to take the bodies. So they had to repeat the autopsies, those who were buried under certain name, the families requested fresh autopsies and DNA identification and this is where this exchange of letters happened between them. And that is the goal, objective, of the letter of Gordon Bacon. This is what I wanted to help you with because here he was providing guide-lines that they cannot take over all of the responsibility upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show a letter by Mr. Odobasic to the chief prosecutor, if I may be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the exact topic that you just told Mr. Karadzic to move on from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will move on to my final topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, the Prosecution experts, did they provide collective reports? What did they combine in those reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidence was led by the Prosecution experts about numerous localities, i.e., numerous mass graves. These reports are collective reports pertaining to certain locations. These collective reports actually explain the method of work on each of the locations as well as collective conclusions of all the individual autopsy reports that pertain to a particular location. Thus, the collective reports are the reflections of individual situations that were established by pathologists. And now we come to the key thing that I've tried to explain all the time. A lot of effort was invested, a lot of work was carried out; however, in order to assess the validity of the collective reports, when I had doubts I had to evaluate all the individual reports. In some situations and in a certain number of cases which I have mentioned here, I realised that individual reports were not presented in the way they should be presented by an expert pathologist, whereas in the collective report, the chief pathologists Clark and Lawrence, I would be free to say that they took it into account all those cases and they represented them with some reservations, albeit. However, they never found it appropriate to correct such individual reports. Very often they provided their own free interpretation of those erroneous reports. I will go back to that a bit later. What is important here is that Haglund and Baraybar are anthropologists and they did their own collective reports with comments. I commented upon their findings; however, they also embarked on some very free interpretations of the findings they saw which went beyond the scope of their own line of work. For example, Mr. Haglund, reporting on Pilica, amongst other things states as follows: The additional bullet wounds on the heads of various victims point to the fact that the fire was opened from a close vicinity or close range. That comment itself goes beyond the scope of his profession. As an anthropologist, he cannot answer - either myself or Clark or Lawrence - how he knows that out of the 10 or 15 wounds, one wound is additional, which means that it could be created three hours, five days, or 15 days after the last in a series. He doesn't have any forensic evidence to prove that an additional wound on the head is indeed an additional wound. Nobody can conclude that. I can't, nobody else can. So this is a free interpretation of a finding which carries a certain connotation before the Court. If something is additional on the head, for example, a wound on the head, if it's subsequent, that means that somebody had an absolute intention either to kill that person, to finish that person off, or to inflict the wound for whatever reason. But in any case, with a good intention. But there is no physical evidence to prove that allegation, apart from the location of the wound itself. This means that the collective reports reflect what was done on the location; however, some comments provided by the authors of those collective reports are very arbitrary in some situations and they are not based on the objectively established facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, when you sum up unreliable or inaccurate, individual reports, can you end up with an accurate collective report? Does a collective report somehow improve the situation of individual reports. In other words, the omissions that were made in individual reports, how do they reflect on a collective report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an expert, I find it very difficult to talk about that. It's up to the Trial Chamber to be the judge of that. However, the individual mistakes, omissions, and comments that exist point to the objections that some other people had and they said that there was a lot of subjectivism and very little objectivism. That was noted in international professional circles. The information that was received from elsewhere, and Lawrence and Clark testified to that as well as Richard Clark [as interpreted], i.e., that they found information about Srebrenica in newspapers and in the local media, I believe that that had a lot of impact on the drafting of the local report -- of the collective report. Because if I find that out of 100 or 280 or 280 people who were exhumed from one location, that all of them were killed, i.e., that they were wounded from fire-arms when they were still alive and that they were intentionally, as it were, killed and then I read a post-mortem findings for all of the casualties and I find out that in 80 per cent of such conclusions, these conclusions are not objectively sustainable because there is no single proof that the injuries were inflicted ante mortem, then there is something wrong with such a report unless we adopt a doctrine and unless we adopt a position or unless conclusions are redacted in the way the legal advisor of the International Tribunal redacted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the co-ordination that we discussed, would that replace such a doctrine? Do the participants owe something to that co-ordination, to that agreement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't comment, but the fact is that I noticed something else and I have to share that with the Trial Chamber, since I've been involved in the cases surrounding Srebrenica for such a long time. Up to 2000, that's how things were described. After the year 2000, when exhumations continued and post-mortems of the bodies that were found in those graves continued, the pathologists who were hired, Siklas [phoen], Sarajlic, and others, took into account the objections, not only mine as an expert, but also of others. They corrected the way they provided their conclusions. Where bodies were skeletonised, they said that the bodies were skeletonised and that it was not possible to establish a cause of death with any degree of reliability. And that was consistent with the findings. Unlike in the other cases where there was no consistency, and there was no consistency, there was no proof of the injuries being inflicted ante mortem. The bodies are skeletonised, and you say that the cause of death is a head injury because there was a defect of -- in the skull, but nobody can prove that the defect was created ante mortem. I'm not denying that that may have been the case, but I cannot accept that that was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this document into evidence. Mr. Mitchell said that he did not have any questions about the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we not admitted it? Is there any document pending?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have no objections to the report. I do object to that letter that was just on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admitted two reports. Is there a third one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to ask the Professor this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your first two reports you referred to expert report in the Popovic case. You do not repeat things, you just refer to them. Would you say that the Popovic case expert report is one and a whole with the first two reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, the expert report that I provided in the Popovic case and the individual reports that I provided in all those cases - there are several such reports because there were six Defence teams and I did some work for each of them - and what I said before the Trial Chamber could be incorporated into these two reports and can be used in your case because we're talking about the same event and we are using the same documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender that report as well, 1D25489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3896, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 20, 52, I asked the Professor whether they made up an organic unity, and that has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, we just heard you, it's at page 49 of today's transcript, criticise Dr. Haglund and Dr. Baraybar for interpreting findings that you say went beyond the scope of their own line of work. Let me ask you, you're not a military expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say "military expert"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what you had in mind? I'm not a military expert. I'm a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And you're not an expert in the type of clothing worn by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not an expert. I don't know what kind of uniforms the BiH army --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking, Professor. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- wore. But what does that have to do with Haglund? I don't understand that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that in a little while, Professor. You're not an expert in the type of headwear worn by members of the BiH, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know whether such experts exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You're not a demographer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you're not an expert in DNA identifications?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in DNA identifications; however, identification is a process in forensic medicine which is a process and in DNA identifications it's only one part of it. But forensic experts do most of the work, and we're talking about anthropological and forensic examinations that are carried out in identifications. That is one of the principal methods in my profession. I'm not exclusively a DNA expert, that would imply something else. I'm a person who performs identification in a forensic practice using DNA reports as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. You take samples and you submit them for DNA analysis, but you are not an expert in the actual process of DNA matching, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, technicians and biologists do that, they are trained. However, I as a forensic expert have to know whether the procedure for DNA identification was carried out properly. If it wasn't carried out properly in compliance with the protocol, as a forensic expert I have to intervene. When I receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, please --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a so-called DNA profile --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- let me stop you there. You said "technicians and biologists do that, they are trained." You are not trained in the process of DNA matching, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, we saw in your reports that your critique of the Prosecution's anthropologist is based on information that you say was pointed out to you by Professor M aria Djuric, the president of the Serbian Anthropological Society. So you consulted Professor Djuric --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- because you're not professionally qualified as an anthropologist, are you? We can see on your CV, no qualifications as an anthropologist; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must repeat and I must tell you again. I don't have qualifications in anthropology to the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's all I asked you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- extent that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- Professor. I know you're part of a process. But I'm asking you, you don't have qualifications --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let me finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to tell you, within the framework of my profession, which is forensic medicine, there is also training and education in the process of identification. One of the elements is the anthropological examination that I also do as part of my specialisation. However, there are people who are more specialised in that. Maria Djuric is one of them and I consult her. And that goes for DNA matching. I consult Professor Oliver Stojkovic, I ask him whether DNA matching was done properly or whether a certain DNA profile matches the DNA profile of the victim. He then takes a look and he tells me: This was not properly done, or, alternatively, he tells me: There is a certain match. As a forensic expert, I have to have information about the process of identification, but it is absolutely allowed to consult people who know more within the area. That's why I shared with you that I consulted Marija Djuric on the matching of bones. You know, Mr. Mitchell, the last time we talked -- I'm put in a situation that I should either accept a report the way it was drafted or to voice my objections to it. For example, it says in the report a 75-year-old male and then I say: Okay, I can accept that, but give me proof that the man was 75.
