In that autopsy report and in that anthropology report, it has to say -- there has to be some proof of the person's age, the person's gender. I didn't have that at that -- therefore, I had to object, and this is what I'm saying. I apologise, but I felt that that -- it was my duty to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The length of the bone was not recorded and that was part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So your answer is: No, you're not qualified as an anthropologist; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? He answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you're not qualified as an archaeologist either, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Can I have 65 ter 1D25488 in e-court, that's page 3 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see here in your report, Professor, that you repeat some of the allegations that were made in some witness statements given to the San Antonio Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have Exhibit P4338 in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're about to see, Professor, is the final report of the San Antonio Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we go to page 4 in both the English and the B/C/S and then over to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, there's actually quite a number of additional statements given to the San Antonio Committee other than the ones that you cited in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you only selected the ones that made criticisms of Dr. Haglund; right? You only repeated those ones in your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not only the ones with criticisms of Dr. Haglund, but where there's criticism of the whole work, of the process, from the moment the exhumations started. Everything that is written here is not only aimed at Haglund, but the entire manner the exhumations and post-mortems were carried out and how they were influenced from out -- from the outside. That's the point. I really appreciate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Dr. Haglund as an expert. I watched him work and we already discussed that, Mr. Prosecutor, when we discussed this in the Vujadin Popovic case, we already discussed this. You showed me the same document and you pointed at the same thing to me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The point was, Professor, when you chose to cite to certain witness statements that were in the San Antonio report, you only chose the critical ones; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the criticism expressed made it possible to improve the quality of work. I believe this criticism to have been objective coming from those individuals over there. I didn't know anything about it when I got the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to page 7. And let me read you the very first sentence under the heading "Findings." So we're not dealing with allegations in witness statements anymore, we're dealing with findings. The very first sentence says: "The responses of the witnesses did not indicate any actual wrong-doing on the part of Dr. Haglund nor anything regarding the exhumations that jeopardised their scientific validity." Now, that's not objective or impartial, is it, Professor, to quote allegations about Dr. Haglund and ignore the actual finding of the committee, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the drift of your question. Am I supposed to give comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm suggesting, Professor, that you've cherry-picked allegations about Dr. Haglund and you've deliberately ignored the findings here in your effort to criticise the Prosecution's evidence.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not my intention or goal to do that or for that to relate to Haglund alone. My criticism of the entire findings that I reviewed concerned other experts who are not mentioned here and who worked in the project later. My approach was not aimed at cherry-picking only the negative aspects. It is very proper and ethically moral of Mr. Haglund, who testified about how findings and conclusions were drafted. You have to know that both in my profession and his the -- that went a bit beyond the pale. So of course, I took into consideration what he wrote, but I had to write what others had to say and what was negative. If Lawrence - Christopher Lawrence isn't mentioned here - but if in his report he says perforating injuries of soft tissue and there is no soft tissue to be found, this is a random conclusion that he made and I had to make a note of that in my report. Of course, up to that point he did do other things, but I had to bring it to the notice of the Trial Chamber that not everything was done properly. And I had to say that it was an error when they said that the projectile was found in the heart, whereas death came about as a result of suffocation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Back to Dr. Haglund, you said you had to write what the others had said. You didn't trust that we could read these in the San Antonio report for ourselves? You thought you'd pick them out and repeat them again in your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you worked with Dr. Haglund at Ovcara farm in 1996, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And in fact, isn't it true that you found Dr. Haglund's work to be so professional that you tried to emulate his methods during your own work at Lake Radonjic in Kosovo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is something I told you the other time. The man did such a wonderful piece of work in 1996, I was there, saw it for the first time, and there's nothing to conceal there. I'm not attacking him because what he did wasn't good. What I am disagreeing with is his opinion. He said what additional injuries were and he said that they were instrumental, and I know that based on his profession and training this isn't something that he can assert, plus there is no evidence to underpin his conclusions. I'm criticising this. I do consider him to be a good professional, but he went beyond the boundaries of his profession in offering these opinions and comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 60, line 2, what is missing is that the Professor mentioned the Hodzici case, 175 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic repeat what he said, it's a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give it to you right now so that we get it correct. Hodzici 05-175. This is the case for which Lawrence said that it was an evident error. So I'm criticising specific aspects of work. I'm not criticising the individual. This was a different person who conducted the autopsy. He produced the collective report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you can see recommendation number 1 of the San Antonio Committee on the screen in front of you. It says: "Evidence of war crimes is overwhelming at each site. A few problems of administration or temporary lapses from a scientific ideal could not jeopardise the overall quality of the evidence and its interpretation at autopsy. Any prosecution of war crimes in Yugoslavia will be on firm scientific grounds. There are literally hundreds of war crime remains that were removed and interpreted by very scientifically sound methods." Now, you just told us, Professor, that your criticisms were aimed not specifically at Dr. Haglund but the whole process, and yet this recommendation number 1 doesn't get mentioned in any of your three reports, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mentioned because I did not have this recommendation at my disposal. At any rate, my understanding of it is that it is a recommendation. The word says that something is being recommended to somebody else, but the recommendation also states under 1: "The evidence of war crimes is overwhelming at each site ..." This is a conclusion; it is not a recommendation. In other words, somebody has jumped into the conclusion that this has to do with war crimes. And the question that I would put to the author of this recommendation: Sir, when you wrote that there is evidence of war crimes, did you read Dusan Janc's report, where he stated that victims which perished before 1995 were brought there at a later date? And can you tell us, were all the victims there the victims of war crimes or are there victims who perished not as a result of the commission of a war crime? Did somebody perish in combat, in armed conflict and similar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, we can --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on this in various ways --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we can all read it for ourselves. Let me just go back to it. You said it's not mentioned in your reports because you didn't have this recommendation at your disposal. Your most recent report is dated August 2012, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you will recall in the Popovic case in 2008, I read you this exact paragraph from this document. So you were aware of it at the time you wrote that August 2012 report, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may have read it out to me, but I don't recall it nor do I have it in writing. I do accept that you read it out to me in Vujadin Popovic in 2000 and whatever the year was when I was here, though I do not really remember it. I'm telling you how this can be interpreted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- forensically speaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- maybe you can tell us how you were able to quote a number of statements directly out of the San Antonio report, and yet you say you didn't have the conclusion three or four pages on in the exact same report? Professor, you don't have to answer that. You left this out deliberately, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. If you'll recall, in Vujadin Popovic I wrote those seven or eight bullet points that were my objections. After that, the Defence for Vujadin Popovic and another team of Defence counsel accessed that cite and then we all looked at it and commented on it. I have nothing to add. I wrote in the report what I thought was relevant for the Chamber to view the matter from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And in your view, for the Chamber to view the matter from both sides, you have to present just one side; right? That's what you're doing here. You're arguing Mr. Karadzic's case for him, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm presenting my positions which I presented before the Karadzic case, before the Popovic case, and those others' methods. As a forensics expert, I'm only dealing with objectively established facts. The only thing I can do is interpret them and comment on them. I'm not talking about numbers. Are they adequately related to location, time-period, et cetera. If Mr. Christopher Lawrence argues that putrefaction is solely related to the conditions in the pit and indirectly through Mr. Karadzic, when answering my questions whether the time of death and time of interment may also have an impact on putrefaction, then he answers affirmatively, it means that in answering questions that would be in favour of the accused he also provided such answers. So I'm not criticising his position; I'm only saying things that are relevant to one position and the other. I'm not only singling out negative aspects; I'm stating positive things. I did not deny the existence of ligatures or executions, but I did say that I disagreed with the position that all of them were the victims of executions. I disagree with the position of Janc that the primary and secondary -- or rather, that the secondary graves contained bodies that were in primary graves only, I disagree with that. I disagree with his position that executions were conducted at several sites. We have information that there were people who were subsequently interred and who died before July 1995. Some fighters were killed around Srebrenica and these individuals were found buried in these graves. We have testimonies of protected witnesses to that effect. This is what I'm discussing. Whether this plays in somebody's hand or not, I'm not interested in that, I'm not going into that. I want to present to the Chamber that there is such evidence or, alternatively, that there is no such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Just to finish off talking about Dr. Haglund, earlier today you were talking about the comment in Dr. Haglund's Branjevo Farm farm report that Mr. McCloskey facilitated the final editing of the autopsy reports. And you said that you believed the legal advisor wanted to skip any steps and to directly tie-in his conclusion, the conclusion with what he was able to see on the ground. This is what Dr. Haglund had to say in this case at transcript 23940. He said: "I had to put that in there because I wanted people to be aware that he didn't make changes at anything, he just went around the world to see the particular pathologists. I had done particular cases, had them look them over, and if there was a change made to these, pathologists made the change, not McCloskey." So that was in this case. Professor, Dr. Haglund is testifying, as luck would have it, today in the Mladic case. And this is what he said this morning about this issue: "... McCloskey took ... all the writings on how -- what the pathologists had done, and he went all over the world ... to see if they needed to have their -- their writings changed or ... if it was the same way it was. And then they would change it, and then he would go on to another country and find other people, so he basically went to the -- all the -- I think there were 30-some pathologists that we had from Turkey, England, the United States, and all over. And ... he carried things around, but Mr. McCloskey, of course, didn't change anything. It was none of his business. He just took it to the pathologist." So, Professor, there's no basis whatsoever for your statement that the Prosecution's legal advisor wanted to skip steps and tie-in his own conclusions with what he saw on the ground, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the case. That I cannot glean from this document. What Peter McCloskey said and what Haglund testified came after what I have just read out. This cannot be interpreted in any way other than that Mr. McCloskey participated in editing the conclusions based on autopsies. Why he did that before that, why did he go abroad, what he was looking for? This can be interpreted in two ways. Was he looking for pathologists who would accept his conclusions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that all of them were alive and were then killed. This is also a possible interpretation. I don't accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- you're in the realm of pure speculation again. I just told you what Dr. Haglund had to say about it. Do you accept that your claim that the Prosecution's legal advisor was trying to tie-in his own conclusions with what he saw on the ground is false?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me once more when did Mr. Haglund say this? The exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund testified under oath before this Trial Chamber and he just said the same thing this morning under oath in front of the Mladic Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did he say so in the case against Vujadin Popovic, the case where I stated these things for the first time? At the time, Prosecutor McCloskey reacted because he was sitting there on the Prosecution side, and when I said this he stood up and said that this wasn't the truth. Therefore, both here and in the Mladic case - because I worked in that case as well - Haglund made the comments that he made and I take them as his comments only. I will not go into detail. However, he said all this after my quoting of his report and in the quote that I relayed, none of what he said was contained. Here, however, you have exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's very clear what the -- what Dr. Haglund's report says. One final thing before the break. Do you recall earlier this morning we were looking at point 12 of Dr. Lawrence's Cancari Road 3 report, talking about post-mortem --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- injuries that tended to obscure peri mortem ones? Well, in your big report, 1D25489 --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- this is at page 212 in the English, you say that Dr. Lawrence's statement is "absolutely arbitrary if not actually malicious." Now, Professor, "malicious" is a very strong word. You're basically calling Dr. Lawrence deliberately dishonest, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the opinion you're referring to? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have the document in e-court, it's 1D2589 [sic], page 212 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe it's 197.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to Cancari Road 3, Prosecutor Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And you say that Dr. Lawrence's statement, the post-mortem injuries tended to obscure peri mortem ones, was "absolutely arbitrary if not actually malicious."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. If you have no evidence of the sequence in which injuries were inflicted, if you have no evidence of an injury having been inflicted at a later date, if you have no evidence of something having been done intentionally and yet you do write all of these things, then the only thing I can say is that it was done malevolently. I simply cannot interpret it otherwise. Why would somebody write that this was done intentionally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the entire body of your legal -- yes, I don't want to comment. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The whole point it was a translation error. It didn't say it was done intentionally. That was cleared up this morning, remember? It doesn't say that in the original English.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless, listen to me carefully. If we omit the word "intentionally" and say that injuries were inflicted post-mortem so as to obscure the injuries inflicted ante-mortem, it's sheer nonsense because there is no evidence to support it. And let's not even talk about intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So that's -- that's your testimony --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professionally speaking, it's unacceptable. Yes, from the position of the profession it's unacceptable. I had at my disposal a translation which said "intentionally inflicted." What I'm saying now, that even if we disregard the translation error, the second part of the sentence is completely unacceptable from the point of view of the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you would still say Dr. Lawrence's comment that post-mortem injuries tended to obscure perimortem injuries, regardless of whether that's done intentionally or not, Dr. Lawrence was being arbitrary or possibly even malicious when he said that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- you're standing by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's not a proper objection for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you, Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I asked you: Is it still your position that Dr. Lawrence's comment that post-mortem injuries tended to obscure perimortem injuries, regardless of whether it's intentional or not, that's arbitrary if not actually malicious, you stand by that comment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we see that passage on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Page 212 in the English, Mr. President. It's in the second-bottom full paragraph, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are two matters I'd like to deal with before we have a lunch break, but in the meantime, Professor Dunjic, you may excuse yourself. We'll resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion to augment Exhibit P1620 and P1621 filed yesterday, on 22nd July 2013. In the motion, the Prosecution seeks to augment the expert report of Witness Patrick Van der Weijden, admitted under seal as P1620 and publicly as P1621, with four photographs which are of "significant higher quality" than those currently contained in the report. Also on the 22nd July 2013, the accused informed the Prosecution and the Chamber via e-mail that he does not oppose the motion. The Chamber has reviewed the new photographs along with the expert report and is satisfied that the four photographs tendered in the motion shall be added to P1620 and P1621 to replace the old photographs. Second, the Chamber has noted the Defence's latest working calendar which Mr. Robinson kindly circulated to the Prosecution and the Chamber's legal staff yesterday, with the proviso that this calendar pertained to "a trial on Counts 2 to 11." The Chamber recalls that on the 11th of July, 2013, the Appeals Chamber issued its judgement on the Prosecution's motion against the Chamber's Rule 98 bis oral ruling on Count 1 -- I should have said Prosecution's appeal. On the 16th of July the accused filed before this Chamber a motion to sever Count 1, and on the 22nd of July, he filed a motion for clarification of the judgement before the Appeals Chamber. The Chamber is concerned about Mr. Robinson's comment that the Defence's working calendar, which covers a number of months and takes us to the end of the Defence case, pertains to Counts 2 to 11 only. At this stage, while making no comment on the merits of the accused's motions that are still pending before the Appeals Chamber and before this Chamber, but simply bearing this mind that all efforts should be made to ensure that the expeditiousness of these proceedings is maintained, the Chamber is of the view that the Defence should also be prepared for the eventuality that in ruling on the motion for clarification, the Appeals Chamber may decide that its judgement was clear that Count 1 is reinstated and also for the possibility that this Chamber may dismiss his motion for severance hereinafter. This means that for witnesses who are scheduled to testify and who may be relevant to Count 1, and the Chamber has noted a few in the working calendar provided, the Chamber expects the Defence to examine them on Count 1 if it so wishes, even if by that time the Appeals Chamber has not ruled on the motion for clarification. We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, we can agree that an expert witness, credible expert witness, should be objective; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And impartial?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Impartial, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that the expert should exercise his or her independent professional judgement in relation to the subject matter of their report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And give clear references for all facts on which your opinion is based?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I want to ask you about the objectivity and impartiality of just three examples of conclusions in your report. The first one, if we can go to your August 2012 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's 1D25488, page 19 in the English, page 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this is number 6, "blindfolds" and personal effects found. And you say: "The presence of these 'blindfolds'" --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Just let me find it. I apologise. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see here you say: "The presence of these 'blindfolds' may be interpreted in several ways ..." And then you list three points. And I want to ask you about each of these three points. First of all, you say: "Many BH Army soldiers (including the 'Mujahedin') wore headbands to distinguish themselves from the other soldiers and to signify that they belonged to a particular unit." We just agreed less than five minutes ago that there should be clear references for all the facts on which your opinion is based, Professor. There's no reference for this statement of fact, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a factual statement and I think that you are familiar with this factual statement because Mr. Karadzic presented that at that point in time when your experts were being heard, last occasion being one which I was present at, and I saw that there. This is a document that we are both familiar with, so that I simply think that I didn't have any need in an additional report to refer to a particular reference number. This is something that I know. I don't even need to use a different term, and that is that in the presence of foreigners in the -- this is something that I know of from newspapers, the presence of foreigners in the B&H army, from the time that I was living in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. But you got this specific factual statement, let me be absolutely clear, you got this from Dr. Karadzic when he said it during the testimony of one of the Prosecution experts; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did he say it, he showed film footage where we saw that. I cannot remember precisely now when that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe you recall that --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just one second --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- that video that Dr. Karadzic showed wasn't admitted into evidence because he couldn't show the provenance of that video. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that I don't know, but if that is so, then that is so. We talked about that on the 8th of December, 2011, when Mr. Lawrence was testifying --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to come to that, Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- blindfolds --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The second bullet point you say -- so you've made the statement of fact. Second bullet point is your opinion where you say: "... after the soft tissue has putrefied, these bands would have 'slipped' over the eyes and face ..." Now, this opinion wasn't in any of the three reports that you did for the Popovic case in 2008 and 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, actually, you are correct. I did not say that anywhere. Now in this augmented report, I wrote that there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when you testified before the Popovic Trial Chamber twice, you didn't suggest this theory that blindfolds could actually be headbands which slipped down after the soft tissue putrefied, you didn't suggest that in your Popovic testimony either, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't recall. If I did not mention it, that does not mean that I did not think it, just that I didn't mention it, I didn't write it down. Simply no one paid attention to that in the same way they did not pay attention to ligatures, whether they were firmly fixed to the arms or not, whether the arms were tied in the front or in the back. You understand? You just simply accept that in a certain way. But when I went into an analysis, when I had a direct question from Dr. Karadzic about these blindfolds and how they can be preserved, then I found a document on Lazete 1 and I could see how those strips looked, what they looked like, what the composition was like, and then in thinking, I came to these things which were presented but which were not admitted as a document in this case. I came to that conclusion, and that is why I did not introduce that or mention it in the Vujadin Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 1D25180.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, this is your August 2009 report which you did for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 57 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, Professor, you'll agree with me that this theory about blindfolds being headbands isn't mentioned anywhere in this report either, is it? We'll come to the list of questions we're looking at here in a minute. I'm just asking you generally, the theory about blindfolds being headbands, it's not in this report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what we're seeing here on page 57 is a list of questions that you drafted for Dr. Karadzic to ask. And you'll see that there's nothing in there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- about blindfolds possibly being headbands either. So in August 2009, this hasn't occurred to you; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: As in "no," it hasn't occurred to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it didn't occur to me, but I did not elaborate in that sense on that fact which was constantly being repeated. But I did after the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses here, your witnesses, expert witnesses, and after the film footage was shown by Dr. Karadzic, and after I got interested in the whole question about who is wearing what kind of bands and so on, then I participated in the writing of this because these are additional questions that were given to me by Dr. Karadzic and I answered them, and that is what the title is of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's be very clear. You wrote three reports for the Popovic case. You testified twice in the Popovic case. And then you wrote a fourth report in August 2009, in each of them specifically talking about the blindfolds, and this theory didn't appear in any of them; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted facts that were available to me. Blindfolds referred to by the Investigator Manning. I just noted the fact without going into an explanation of the blindfolds, in the same way that I did not go into any explanations about ligatures on the arms and legs. Had I been put that question and had a special analysis on that been necessary, then I would have done that work and I would have looked at the annexes B, C, in order to acquaint myself with that material. I did not do that up until this report of last year because that was when a specific question was put to me regarding those blinds -- blindfolds. And that was when I then began to think about it and to perceive the significance and the way all of that was. Somebody who had more information about that, as Mr. Karadzic did, about who is wearing what in which way -- well, I'm a civilian, I did not participate in any war. So I did not know what kind of things were being worn. So it's logical that I had to think about that and go into the matter in more detail without any further conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The 8th of December, 2011, you were sitting in court during Dr. Lawrence's evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you saw the video that Mr. Karadzic played; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you heard Mr. Karadzic explain that video to the Judges and say: "Dr. Lawrence confirmed to us that he had not been made aware of our customs of war or of this custom of the Islamic fighters wearing headbands. That is one thing. Secondly, that fully coincides with the findings of such objects in the mass graves." So on the day that Dr. Lawrence testified, on the 8th of December, 2011, you became fully aware of Mr. Karadzic's case theory on what these blindfolds are; correct? So --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- then when you say for the first time ever nine months later you include this theory in your report in August 2012; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, were you specifically asked to include this theory in your report of August 2012 to try and give it an air of respectability, or did you decide all by yourself to help Dr. Karadzic out by putting it in there after you heard him suggest it to Dr. Lawrence on the 8th of December, 2011?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I wrote in my second report on the 26th of August, 2012, I also wrote the reasons why I did that. The second report is written at the request of Mr. Karadzic, who specifically put certain questions to me and that is written down. And so one of the questions was question 6, I quote, blinds and found personal items, and then since certain things are referred to here, I looked at what Mr. Lawrence Hamilton said on the -- when he testified on the 8th. And then I linked that report that you referred to, and to me that had a completely different connotation in relation to what I was doing before because I did not pay attention to the blindfolds. I accepted blindfolds as a fact, that's what was said, a blindfold. But then when I began to analyse what Mr. Karadzic said and what was written in the reports, what was objectively possible, that the blindfolds could have a certain different meaning, as we heard that they did have a different meaning, I had to take that probability or that possibility into account and that is why I wrote it down; I'm not concealing that. I did not think about that at all. I didn't think about it before. Had I thought about that before, I would have elaborated more on that matter also in the Vujadin Popovic case. In the document, for example, on Lazete 01 - doesn't matter now - finding a strip of fabric in the pocket of the clothing. So it was seen in some other cases and then in this case it was found in a pocket of an item of clothing. How would you interpret that? I had to refer to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We'll get to that --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I became interested and I started to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- particular blindfold in one moment. Maybe I can be a little bit clearer for you. Professor, what I'm suggesting is this section of your report isn't an expert analysis at all. It's you simply repeating the Defence case theory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. I think that this is an expert report, an expert analysis. I, as a forensics expert, am answering questions that are put to me. As for whose case that is, that is something that I am not dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's talk about the specific individual who you mention in the third paragraph or the third bullet point. Where you say: "The fact that one strip was found in the pocket of the individual's clothes, LZ-01659-2, bright pink fabric similar to the other blindfolds, imposes the conclusion that this person wanted somehow to hide their identity of belonging to a unit." Now, that conclusion that somebody wants to hide their identity of belonging to a unit has got nothing whatsoever to do with your expertise as a pathologist, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, you are right. I cited the report, I cited this document, this is the source document, where all the blindfolds are referred to in annex D, analysing the blindfolds where they were found. Here it says only head. Here it says blindfold in the grave; and here it says in the pocket. Then I was thinking, as a forensics person, why somebody would keep that same kind of strip that was found on a corpse around the head in -- would keep it in their pocket. So I agree that perhaps I stepped out of the domain of the forensics profession and provided a kind of explanation or an assumption as to why something like that was done. I do grant you that, in that sense. Just as Christopher Lawrence Hamilton, your expert in certain cases gives free interpretations about the origin of some injuries for which he does not have objective proof. I have objective proof in the pocket, evidence found. In his case, Mr. Reference to Hodzic, he said that there were perforating wounds on the soft tissue and that could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's -- Professor, let's stay on --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- possibly be the cause of death and there is no soft tissue, so that is in the same -- in the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's stay on point. We're talking about this individual and this blindfold. Okay? Now, when you came up with this theory about the blindfold after hearing Dr. Karadzic say it in court one day, did you look at any witness statements that talked about the blindfolding of prisoners at the Orahovac school, which is associated with the Lazete 1 grave? Did you look at any witness statements?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Excuse me, but other than statements that are referred to, I did not read any other statements. What is cited in my report, but other than that I did not have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me read you two very short bits of evidence from this case from two survivors of the Orahovac executions. This is from Witness KDZ064, whose evidence is P769 in this case. And he said, talking about in the Orahovac school: [As read] "When the order came, they brought a bag of rags or strips of cloth that were maybe some 50 centimetres wide -- 5 centimetres wide, or rather, 15 centimetres wide and they asked prisoners to put these blindfolds on each other." So you haven't heard that statement before, about the Bosnian Serb soldiers bringing --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is KDZ039, who's another survivor of the Orahovac executions, who said in his evidence, which is P3940: "When we were supposed to go out, two soldiers brought this kind of thing, some kind of cloth cut into pieces and they put it by the entrance door and they said to these two men, 'Now, who is going to be the two men tying people's eyes, and then you will have water to drink,' and then two of our men volunteered." Then he goes on: "They would get blindfolded, they would drink water, and then we would leave the hall." So you hadn't consulted any eyewitness testimony when you included this theory in your August 2012 report for the first time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay, if we could have 65 ter 25433 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, Professor, before you concluded that this individual with the strip of cloth in his pocket was trying to hide the fact that he was in a unit, did you look at his autopsy report? I don't think there's a translation, unfortunately, so I'll have to read the relevant section to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 26 of the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you just briefly explain to us, Professor, what a fluoroscope is? It's a type of x-ray, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a type of x-ray done on certain parts of the body. This is one such image, the image of I don't know what. I believe that this is somewhere in the chest, I assume, and the shadow, the darker shadow with sharp edges looks like a projectile trace, or rather, a segment, a part of a projectile embedded in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rifle projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go back to page 1, you will see, Professor, that the cause of death for this individual is a gun-shot injury to the head and trunk. Now, do you agree with that conclusion, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, that would mean that. The cause of death may have been a gun-shot wound or the injury of the head and chest on a condition that the injuries were inflicted ante-mortem. However, there's no proof of that in the autopsy report --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, it says -- Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It says at the top: "A complete and intact body, well preserved, with the skin and soft tissue surviving in all areas and also all of the internal organs." A body in that state of preservation, you would surely be able to tell what the cause of death was; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. When was the autopsy carried out, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The 22nd of August, 2000 --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of August, 2000 -- or rather, the 22nd August, 2000, and now I would like you to display the description of putrefaction changes to see whether that was indeed the case or should we just accept this at face value. I would like to ask for the proof that the person is aged between 30 and 70. I would like to ask for the proof that the person was between 174 and 179 centimetres tall. There has to be proof in the autopsy report and then I would be able to reply to you and tell you that everything is correct. Because if somebody died in 1995 with a projectile in their head and in the trunk or in the chest because they were wounded at the time, how is it possible five years later for the soft tissues to be preserved without any putrefaction changes? As a forensic expert, I have never seen any such thing. It may be preserved, there may be signs of putrefaction, yes, it may be saponified and altered in many different ways, yes, that may be the case. Are you following me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm following you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so the cause of death is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's just move on briefly. The description here says that this man had three bullet-holes in the back of his chest and two exit defects at the front of his chest. So that means he was shot in the back; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have some pictures of this body?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, we're about to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can go to page 23, Professor, and the summary says: "This man had a blindfold around his head made from a strip of pink cloth knotted at the back." So you'd agree that this individual actually was executed because he's wearing a blindfold; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to fully agree before I reviewed everything else if this is the same body that we're talking about. First of all, there's putrefaction visible here. Secondly, this blindfold across the forehead may correspond to a blindfold although it is around the forehead. And the injuries that were identified in the chest and in the head may have happened at any moment and it cannot be excluded that they were inflicted in a moment of execution had the person indeed been executed. This is the way I'm thinking at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. So your --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- based on these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So your expert opinion, Professor, is that this individual who was shot in the back with a blindfold on - and we saw the bullets in his chest and pelvis - you can't tell what the cause of death was? That's your expert opinion? We're going to come to the strip of cloth in the pocket in a minute.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So "yes," you can't tell what the cause of death is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can only assume what the exact cause of death was. One can assume that it may have been related to the injuries in the head and chest regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I read you two bits of evidence, the Bosnian Serb soldiers brought a bag of rags or strips of cloth to the Orahovac school and Muslim prisoners used that material to blindfold each other before they were executed. So, Professor, do you think it's plausible that this individual was wearing a blindfold taken from a bag of rags brought to the Orahovac school by Bosnian Serb soldiers that is made of identical material as an Islamic headband that was in his pocket at the time that he was shot? Being do you think that's a plausible explanation, that the bag of rags for the blindfolds and the Islamic headband in his pocket just happened to be the exact same material?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's really not up to me to be the judge of that, whether that's just a coincidence or not. I simply cannot give you any comment. It may well be the case, but it doesn't have to be. It doesn't have to say that the materials are the same, that they're identical. There is a detailed description of the colours of those headbands and the appearance --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, it says in the autopsy report - if we go back to page 1 - that they're identical. So, Professor, let me suggest this to you: Isn't the most plausible explanation for what happened was that this prisoner was one of the ones I mentioned earlier who was blindfolding other prisoners and who picked up a pile of strips of cloth out of that bag, stuck them in his pocket and was blindfolding other prisoners; and when it came his turn, there's one strip left in his pocket. Isn't that the most obvious explanation, Professor, rather than the Islamic headband?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very possible. It is very possible. That theory is quite plausible. I cannot reject it, of course I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 1D25488 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, this is your August 2012 report again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have page 26 in English, 22 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to your statement that if bodies are found in civilian clothes, it does not necessarily mean that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Many civilians in this period were armed and active in Territorial Defence in accordance with the doctrine of the former SFRY. You can see that section?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And again, this is a statement of fact without any citation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a factual statement. I lived there. I was a member of the civilian protection myself, I was a civilian. As for the military doctrine of the SFRY - and mind you, I had served in the army - it was the military doctrine to prepare civilians for war and to provide them with certain weaponry, perhaps not uniforms. I know it because I am a witness of that time. Anybody who resided in the former republics of Yugoslavia can confirm that. Being members of the Territorial Defence, everybody had to be there, we had to do all sorts of things, learn all sorts of things as members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, you did some autopsies in Kosovo in 1998 of individuals killed by the KLA at Racak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you misspoke. Could you please be more precise. I performed autopsies in Kosovo of the people who were killed by the KLA? No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I did misstate --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I performed autopsies of persons who were members of the KLA and who rebelled against the legitimate military and police forces of the then-Republic of Serbia, or rather, the SRY. I did perform those autopsies and that was what you refer to as Racak. There were 40 bodies all together and I testified about that here at the Tribunal. I was a team member together with Helena Ranta and two forensic experts from Belarus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I apologise, Professor, I was actually referring to the 39 individuals who were killed near Lake Radonjic in 1998.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's something entirely different. That was in the Haradinaj case. I did work there. I was the one who did those autopsies as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The victims in that case were wearing civilian clothes, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever is a convenient moment, I would like to correct something in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do it now then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 86, line 3, it seems that the Professor stated that the theory is quite plausible. Does that mean desirable? He said that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, possible or credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Very possible, not plausible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that makes much difference. Thank you, in any event. Shall we continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, are you not tendering the autopsy report we saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I would like to. I apologise, I missed it. That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, no objection with respect to those pages that were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6461, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, the 39 people who were killed at Lake Radonjic were people of Serb and Albanian ethnicities who were thought to have been killed by the KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is what you said about the significance of civilian clothes in that instance. This is a statement you gave in June -- November 2001, where you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, is this in e-court where we could follow this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yeah, it's 65 ter 25380, it's page 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There's just one very simple quote, Professor, where you say -- you're talking about the 39 cases and you say: "All the above-mentioned bodies were in civilian everyday clothing which would possibly indicate they had been dragged from their homes or work-places." So in that case, where the KLA were the perpetrators and there were Serbs among the victims, civilian clothing meant they were possibly dragged from their homes; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me hear your next question so as to be able to expand on my answer. Tell me what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, my next question is: You've gone out of your way in your report in this case to argue that victims dressed in civilian clothes could still be soldiers. So the significance of civilian clothes to you, Professor, appears to depend on the identity of the perpetrator and of the victim; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Namely, we're discussing Mr. Karadzic's case and I said -- in view of some allegations of the fact that people were in civilian clothes, I said that civilian clothing doesn't mean that people wearing it are not soldiers. According to the prevalent doctrine and according to what we knew in 1991 and 1992 when the war started in my country. I know that. What you are talking about now, the Kosovo case, where I said that the people were civilians has nothing to do with that. I performed those autopsies with my team and I did the investigation. I performed the investigation that you normally do at the location, around the location, together with the investigative judge. That's how things are done in my country. And finally, we carried out exhumations of post-mortems and identifications. Therefore, for all the 39 victims, we knew who they were, where they had been dragged from - they were dragged from their houses and apartments. There were two sisters, one was 70, the other was 75 years old, they were in civilian clothes. Of course they were not soldiers. Just like the postman who had been killed. He was a postman, he wore a uniform, he was among the first ones to be killed. There were no armed formations there, there were no Serbian armed formations in Kosovo. On the other hand, the Albanian or armed formations, the KLA, they didn't have uniforms at first, they started wearing them only later. This is just for your information. So I'm not making any distinction in terms of the ethnic structure. I'm just drawing conclusions based on what I had an opportunity to see, to investigate, and to conclude. So if you are asking me whether a 70-year-old woman could be a soldier, I would say it doesn't make sense. If you asked me the same thing about a 35-year-old man who was found near Kravica, I will tell you it is possible because I know what was happening in Bosnia. This is the information that your experts also had from newspapers. I lived in Belgrade and those things were happening 200 or 300 kilometres away from Belgrade. Therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But you thought it was important to make sure the Trial Chamber knew in this case that civilian clothing didn't necessarily mean they were civilians. You thought it was important for them to know that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I believe because I respect this Tribunal, I respect the Prosecution, and I want them to have all the information before them to be able to render the right judgement. There was a woman who testified that a man was killed by a shell, a shell fell in front of his house, he was there and he was also counted as a victim of the Srebrenica genocide. I'm not denying the fact that he was a civilian and that he was among those victims who were civilians. I'm not denying that. I'm just saying that among those "civilians" was a large number of people. Your protected witnesses, the witnesses whom I mentioned, they were all in civilian clothes and they had to join the 281, 20 -- 102nd or 3rd or whatever brigade or division or whatever they were called in Srebrenica. For example, if somebody forced me to join a brigade, I would still be wearing civilian clothes but I would become a soldier. But to show due respect towards you and the Tribunal, I had to say that. I am saying that not only civilians were killed as civilians nor were soldiers killed as soldiers. This is what I'm claiming and this is the only reason why I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go back to 65 ter 1D25488, page 18 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we do that I would ask that this document that was just referred to, this report concerning the -- Kosovo be admitted because I think it shows the sex of the victims that were examined by Dr. Dunjic and corroborates his answer. So I think as long as it's been referred and shown, it ought to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty with it, Mr. Mitchell. Page, what, 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I think we would like to have this whole report admitted because you have to look at different individuals to see that several of them are women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it to Mr. Karadzic. If he's interested in it, then he can lead that evidence. Shall we continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. 1D25488. Page 18 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, on this page you suggest that there are two explanations why some of the individuals in Srebrenica-related graves were wearing winter clothing. The first suggestion is that they were most probably killed in winter before or much later than the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995; or that the time of death at one site differs and burials were carried out on several occasions. You can see those two conclusions in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that, yes. I saw your exhibits showing winter clothes when you heard Professor Lawrence, if I'm not mistaken, I don't know what the exhibit number is. Therefore, what I included in my report is what I claimed then and what I still claim. Winter clothes worn in summer may be interpreted in a certain way. Within the facts adjudicated so far and especially what was said by Dusan Janc about subsequent burials at different times and the different times of death, about the fact that victims were found in many localities that had been killed in 1993 and 1994, it is absolutely plausible to conclude that it was winter when they were killed and not the hot July of 1995. It is a logical conclusion. There is no tendentiousness there. This just corroborates the putrification and the times of death that I've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Professor. You've given two explanations. The third explanation is that these people were actually wearing winter clothes in July 1995 when they left Srebrenica, right? That's the third explanation? And perhaps I can assist you by reminding you of your testimony in the Popovic case at transcript 27876 in that case, where you said: "I am aware that these people were outdoors, that it was war, and that it was quite possible for these people to wear winter clothes even in the summer." So you know about this third explanation, you just didn't include it in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, that third possibility. Therefore, in addition to that one, there are these two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have Prosecution Exhibit 4909, page 10 -- sorry, page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're going to see, Professor, is a still image from footage taken in Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995. And you can see there, can't you, that a number of the men are wearing sweaters, jackets, and hats on their head; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you may -- yes, that's what I wanted. These are not winter clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: These are not winter clothes? A woollen jumper, a jacket --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a thin jacket. It's a thin jumper. This is a leather jacket. This is a suit jacket the other person is wearing. This is not winter clothes. I don't know if somebody may wear clothes like this during winter, but what you imply under that is woollen jumpers, woollen trousers, woollen socks. This is typical of our people that they would have woollen, knitted socks, then underclothes, two or three pairs of underclothes underneath trousers, and then of course thick jackets and coats. That's what you wear in winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So in your view, wearing multiple layers of clothes is a definite sign that it was cold; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the custom in winter or cold spells, let's say, in late autumn, winter, early spring, whenever one spends a lot of time outdoors and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, I referred earlier to the autopsy reports of the 40 Kosovo Albanians killed at Racak, that the alleged perpetrators in that case were the Serbian police, correct, the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you were told when you went to do those 40 autopsies that the victims may well be KLA terrorists; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell us that. They only told us that the persons killed were Albanians who had previously killed two policemen and that they were about to go and arrest these Albanians who were in civilian clothes. Now, if you asked me about the civilian clothes that they wore, I can tell you right away that they all had civilian clothes. However, beneath these civilian clothes, these people who lived outdoors had long johns and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and boots and they all had identical long johns of the type that the military wear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25381 in e-court, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, Professor, this is a statement you gave on the 29th and 30th of November, 2001. Do you recognise your signature down at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- well, this is what you say on that page: "On the afternoon of the 19th of January, 1999, I commenced the autopsies after being briefed by the investigating judge, Danica Marinkovic. She told us that we were doing autopsies on KLA terrorists, that they had killed policemen ..." So you were told that these people on whom you were doing autopsies were KLA terrorists; right? This is your statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we see in this statement your view in this case, in the case of the KLA terrorists, that the extra layers of clothing had nothing to do with the cold even though you actually say it was cold at the time. And you say: "The long underpants and trousers seemed strange to me and nothing to do with the cold, but if you take off one layer of clothing then you think you see a different person. Even though it was cold at the time, I find that the extra layers of trousers were strange and in my opinion had nothing to do with the weather." So in the Racak case where it actually was cold, winter clothing has nothing to do with the cold; but in Srebrenica, winter clothing can only mean cold? Professor, you've completely changed your position in these cases to support the position that's most favourable to the perpetrators; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Can you please find that reference for me where I said that it had nothing to do with the cold? Now, the point of the matter with Racak is that the civilians had military long johns on them, all of which were procured from the same supply, as well as boots. And one could tell by that that they spent time outdoors. They were all in civilian clothes while, in fact, they were KLA members. This is what I'm saying. Please do not put things in my mouth that aren't true. And I said this in very precise terms in my statement in that case as well. These were people who had two or three layers of long johns and trousers to be able to withstand the cold. However, what matters is that they wanted to pass themselves off as civilians and that they were being supplied, from abroad or from wherever, with long johns, with these padded boots, et cetera. It's a completely different issue compared to this one where people in Srebrenica were recovered with as many layers of clothes. The conclusion that I draw on that basis is that these are not only civilians that we are dealing with because wearing a uniform is not the only hallmark of one's membership of the army. People in Bosnia were also compelled to join certain military units. I only commented on the position expressed by John Clark that not everyone can be tied in with a war conflict and that they were all civilians. But they were not all civilians because Helena Ranta, when she worked on the Racak case together with me, she said, "They are all civilians." And I told her, "Ms. Ranta, to you they may be all civilians, however, according to what they were doing they were not. But let's establish our finding and the finding is the one that will be judged by a panel of judges as to its credibility." If gunpowder residue is found on the hands of a victim, as was in the case in Racak, what does that mean? The person is a victim who obviously opened fire previously while wearing civilian clothes. It's a completely different matter, so please do not comment on my expert report in this way. I was an expert in that case and I'm an expert in this case, and I know absolutely well what I said at the time and what I said now and what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's move to one discrete area before we finish today. You testified yesterday about your inability to examine some of the artefacts from the mass graves because they had been disposed of. Now, you first learned on the 3rd of June, 2009, about the disposal of these artefacts; correct? That was at transcript page T 41736 in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I wrote about this, unless I'm mistaken, Mr. Mitchell --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you testified --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Vujadin Popovic. At that time I received the report from Mr. Zoran Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you testified yesterday that -- at transcript page 41736 that you learned that on the 3rd of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3 July 2009, the counsel for Vujadin Popovic, in the case -- et cetera, et cetera. Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So, the three reports you had done in the Popovic case, in April 2008, in September 2008, and April 2009, were all completed before you found out that some of these artefacts had been destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So if you first learned of the destruction of the artefacts after you completed the reports, you didn't ask to inspect any of those artefacts during the completion of your reports; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So we can agree then that the fact that you didn't actually look at these artefacts didn't hinder your preparation of those three reports in any way; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. I didn't even entertain the idea that some of these artefacts existed. It was only when I found out that they were destroyed did I realise that they had existed but were now destroyed. As you can tell, it's the 3rd of July, 2009, in other words, at the end of trial against Vujadin Popovic, whereas I completed my work in late August 2009, this collated big report for Mr. Karadzic. So I thought that it should be entered into that report as well because that was practically the last document that had been disclosed by the Prosecution in the Popovic case. It all seemed to have been coming in successively. As information was coming in, I had to provide ad hoc comments. We didn't yet discuss the DNA that we hadn't received from Parsons to check identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, in February of 2010 we disclosed a list of these artefacts to Mr. Karadzic, and in the cover letter advised him that these items were disposed of because the majority were potential health hazards because they were in the process of degrading or decomposing. Now, you yourself are aware of the difficulties in preserving biological material that's come out of a mass grave, aren't you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Because when you did the autopsies of the 39 bodies for Lake Radonjic, you took samples from those bodies, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you took them back to Belgrade and then you put them in a fridge at the Forensic Institute there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my institute, upon approval from the investigating judge, Danica Marinkovic, we were given approval to take these artefacts to our institute and to store them away there because we didn't know what would happen in the meantime. These samples were to serve for our DNA analysis that we subsequently conducted in Spain and this was paid for by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, well, the ICTY asked you in 2001 to send the samples to Madrid for testing. And when you went to open the fridge, you found that the labels on eight of the 39 samples had smudged and you couldn't tell what they were; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you went and put those eight samples in the bin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't throw them in the bin. Some of the samples had their numbers preserved and others had to be destroyed. We couldn't use them for our analysis because putrefaction progressed. It was an error that we did at the time, I confess that. We placed them in the fridge but there were power outages, humidity developed in the bags, and the numbers were obliterated. And, professionally speaking, we made the mistake because we did not otherwise label these blood and tissue samples. And the samples that we took to Spain, I took them myself together with an ICTY investigator. We took them to Spain and we produced a report. Mistakes were made, I admit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, let me --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was under my leadership and we did make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You've missed out a couple of key points in that story. The samples that went to Spain, the remaining samples, were contaminated and couldn't be used, right, so the bodies had to be re-exhumed and new samples taken; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you state it in these terms, that's how it turns out to be, but the Court has to be well-informed. This means that at the time, in 2001, when the samples were taken, it was not possible to conduct DNA analysis on the bones that had further decomposed. The results were imprecise and poor. At the time the method was not good enough. It was ultimately perfected in the IMP labs in Sarajevo and in Madrid because they didn't have experience, and we're talking about the period of 1998/1999. The bones were stored in a fridge, there were power outages on occasion because of the situation we were in, mold caught, and the tissue itself was further contaminated and the routine DNA testing could not return positive results. That was why samples were ultimately taken again because the method was perfected in the meantime. You can ask Parsons about that. Exhumations were done, samples were taken, in order to confirm some of the identifications that we had arrived at through classical means or conventional means without the DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. One final question, Professor. Yesterday you testified at transcript page 21736 that: If certain artefacts are either destroyed or lost or not properly described, I as a professional deem this to be showing disrespect to a profession as well as a negligent attitude towards the Court and the Tribunal. So, Professor, wouldn't you agree that given your own experience with the difficulties in storing biological material, rather than being disrespectful or negligent, it's actually perfectly appropriate to dispose of an artefact that's a potential health hazard if appropriate documentary and photographic records are maintained; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to respond right away. I agree that any risk of a health hazard has to be avoided. However, it requires that I inform you, as a Judge, that we will be destroying a number of artefacts but that that would not have any bearing on our investigation so far. What happened is this, we had this situation: One-third was destroyed, the rest were relocated, and nobody was informed of it. And then subsequently we find out that somebody analysed it, that it was a health hazard, et cetera. All right. Whoever was involved in such a process would be understandable; however, there has to be a document in writing, as was the case here, there has to be a written document from a prosecutor or a judge which will state: Yes, we agree with the opinion of Mr. Dunjic, all of it has to be destroyed. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But we can agree, where there's a health hazard, it's perfectly acceptable to dispose of an artefact if there are proper documentary and photographic records; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can stop here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned. Yes, it has been a long day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Long day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of July, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.54 p.m.,
